theme: published decipherment claims, acceptance criteria and unicity distance
question: Does Yajnadevam's Sanskrit key read the Indus corpus more readily than rearrangements of its own values, and does his unicity-distance argument hold for the representation the key fixes?
outcome: With two-consonant stems, random consonant strings at Sanskrit letter frequencies are readable from attested DCS lemmas in 91.8-96.4% of cases at lengths 4-16 and from Monier-Williams headwords in 98.5-99.7%; with one-consonant stems every non-empty skeleton is readable. The key reads 94.8% (DCS) of 1,859 unique texts, above all 1,000 within-stratum permutations (mean 88.9%, max 94.1%), but within-stratum hill-climbing reaches 99.4-99.6%; Monier-Williams: key 96.0%, permutations 93.9%, fitted 99.5%. Held-out redundancy is 0.573 for full text and 0.167 for the fifteen-class skeleton; the preprint's formula gives at most 1,980 consonants (about 790-1,760 under corrections) against 473 in the 50 longest texts. 69.2% of 1,747 published readings match the key's skeleton; most departures add unwritten consonants.
challenge: The readability criterion is an emulation with Monier-Williams and DCS lexicons and a small ending set; the preprint's practice adds further freedom (inserted consonants, sandhi, other dictionaries), which would only raise the acceptance rate.
remedy: Exact reproduction of the app's key and inherent-vowel rule, independent verification of skeletons and readability shares, local-only raw sources.
retry_when: A proposed key specifies an acceptance criterion with measured redundancy, or a new lexicon-free criterion is defined; repeating dictionary-readability tests without random-string calibration does not inform.
